title: Running PostgreSQL: processes, configuration, roles and connections
goal: By the end you can name the processes and memory a PostgreSQL server is made of and say why each connection costs a process, find the data directory and its config files, change a setting and know whether it needs a reload or a restart, predict what pg_hba.conf does with a connection, give a service a role with only the privileges it needs, and tell when a pooler belongs in front of the database.

warmup.q: Ops wants to raise `max_connections` from 100 to 2,000 "so the pods never run out". On PostgreSQL, what does each extra open connection cost the server?
options: About a hundred bytes in a connection table, because one server process runs every session
One thread inside the server process, sharing all of its memory
A separate operating-system process, forked for that connection, with its own private memory, alive until the client disconnects
Nothing until the connection starts a transaction
warmup.why: PostgreSQL forks one backend process per connection and keeps it until the client disconnects. An idle one held about 1.5 MB of private memory in this lesson's measurement, more once it has cached catalog entries and plans, and opening one took 3 to 15 ms. Shared memory is also sized from max_connections at start-up. There is no thread-per-session mode to switch to: the thread answers describe Oracle's threaded mode or MySQL, not PostgreSQL.

sections.h: A server is a postmaster, a process per connection, and shared memory
sections.body:
Start the course's database and list the processes inside its container. Nine are running before anyone has connected:

```text
  PID  PPID   RSS CMD
    1     0 33348 postgres -c shared_preload_libraries=pg_stat_statements -c track_io_timing=on
   75     1  7604 postgres: io worker 0
   76     1  6948 postgres: io worker 1
   77     1  6248 postgres: io worker 2
   78     1  6308 postgres: checkpointer
   79     1  6440 postgres: background writer
   81     1 10636 postgres: walwriter
   82     1  9776 postgres: autovacuum launcher
   83     1  8988 postgres: logical replication launcher
```

Process 1 is the **postmaster**, the program `postgres` itself. It opens port 5432 and a Unix socket, creates the shared memory, starts the other processes, and from then on mostly waits. Every other process is its child (PPID 1), and each has one job:

- the checkpointer writes changed pages from memory to the data files every few minutes, so that crash recovery can start from there instead of from the start of the write-ahead log (the WAL, the file every change is appended to before COMMIT returns; the database internals track builds one in "Write-ahead logging and crash recovery");
- the background writer writes some changed pages early, so a query that needs a free page in memory rarely has to write one out first;
- the WAL writer flushes, every 200 ms, WAL that sessions put in memory but did not flush themselves;
- the autovacuum launcher starts workers that remove dead row versions, the old copies an UPDATE leaves behind ("MVCC: versions, snapshots and VACUUM" in the internals track), and that refresh the planner's statistics;
- the logical replication launcher starts workers for subscriptions (lesson 16);
- the three io workers, new in PostgreSQL 18, do the reads of the new asynchronous I/O system (`io_method = worker`).

There is no statistics collector any more: since PostgreSQL 15 the counters behind the `pg_stat_*` views live in shared memory.

When a client connects, the postmaster calls `fork()`, and the copy becomes a **backend**: one process that serves that one connection until it disconnects (`fork` is in "Processes: fork, exec, wait and signals", lesson 2 of the OS track). Its ps line says who it serves: `postgres: sfz course [local] SELECT` is user sfz, database course, the Unix socket, running a SELECT.

Two kinds of memory sit around these processes. **Shared memory** is created once by the postmaster, and every child inherits it: the buffer pool `shared_buffers` (128 MB of 8 KB pages by default), the WAL buffers and the lock table, 152 MB on this server. Every backend reads and writes table pages there, so a page one session loaded is a hit for the next. Private memory belongs to one backend: catalog caches, plans, and `work_mem`, up to 4 MB by default for each sort or hash in a query. Private memory is why a connection is not free; the last section measures it.

Keep this picture for the whole lesson: a postmaster that listens and forks, a ring of helpers, one block of shared memory, and one backend per client. The stepper follows one connection through it.

sections.h: One directory, made by initdb, holds the data and the settings
sections.body:
Everything a PostgreSQL server knows lives in one directory, the **data directory** (often called PGDATA, after its environment variable). The program `initdb` creates it: run as the `postgres` OS user, it lays out the folders, writes the system catalogs and the config files, and stops. Its output on PostgreSQL 18, trimmed:

```text
Data page checksums are enabled.

creating directory /tmp/pgdemo ... ok
creating subdirectories ... ok
selecting default "max_connections" ... 100
selecting default "shared_buffers" ... 128MB
creating configuration files ... ok
running bootstrap script ... ok

Success. You can now start the database server using:

    pg_ctl -D /tmp/pgdemo -l logfile start
```

The first line is new in 18: initdb turns page checksums on unless you pass `--no-data-checksums`, so a page damaged on disk fails loudly when it is read instead of returning wrong rows. `pg_ctl start` (or `postgres -D /tmp/pgdemo`) then serves the directory. PostgreSQL calls one data directory and its server a **cluster**: one set of databases, roles and settings. Run initdb twice, start both on different ports, and you have two independent servers.

A few names inside matter. `base/` holds one folder per database, named by the database's OID: course is `base/16492`, and table payments is the file `base/16492/17439`, which grows in 1 GB pieces. `global/` holds what the whole cluster shares, such as the list of databases and the roles. `pg_wal/` holds the WAL in 16 MB files named `000000010000000000000002` and up. `pg_xact/` records which transactions committed. At the top sit the config files.

`postgresql.conf` lists about 350 settings, nearly all commented out at their defaults. `ALTER SYSTEM SET work_mem = '16MB'` does not edit it: it writes `postgresql.auto.conf`, which the server reads after postgresql.conf, so it wins. A `-c name=value` on the server's command line wins over both. Nothing applies until the server rereads the files, and what a reread achieves depends on the setting's **context**, a column of `pg_settings`:

| context | settings | a change takes effect |
|---|---|---|
| internal | 20 | never: fixed at build or initdb time (block_size, data_checksums) |
| postmaster | 70 | after a restart (shared_buffers, max_connections, listen_addresses) |
| sighup | 105 | after a reload, `SELECT pg_reload_conf()` (checkpoint_timeout) |
| backend, superuser-backend | 6 | after a reload, in sessions started later (log_connections) |
| superuser | 52 | after a reload, or `SET` by a superuser (log_min_duration_statement) |
| user | 151 | after a reload, or `SET` by anyone in one session (work_mem) |

A reload sends the postmaster a SIGHUP, which it passes on to every child, and each rereads the files. A restart-only setting that changed only gets `pending_restart = true` and a log line, `parameter "shared_buffers" cannot be changed without restarting the server`.

Which settings first? On a dedicated server:

| setting | default | start with | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `listen_addresses` | localhost | the interfaces apps use | localhost refuses every remote client (the Docker image sets `'*'`) |
| `max_connections` | 100 | 100 to 300 | each one can be a process, and shared memory is sized for it |
| `shared_buffers` | 128MB | 25% of RAM | the buffer pool; the OS page cache holds more, and above 40% rarely helps |
| `effective_cache_size` | 4GB | 50 to 75% of RAM | allocates nothing: it tells the planner how much data is probably cached |
| `work_mem` | 4MB | 16 to 64MB | per sort or hash, per backend: 200 backends × 3 sorts × 64 MB is about 38 GB |
| `maintenance_work_mem` | 64MB | 512MB to 1GB | VACUUM and CREATE INDEX; each autovacuum worker may take it |
| `wal_level` | replica | replica | enough WAL for standbys and archiving (lesson 16) |
| `max_wal_size` | 1GB | 4 to 16GB | a checkpoint starts when this much WAL piles up; too small and they come every few seconds |
| `checkpoint_timeout` | 5min | 15min | fewer checkpoints write fewer full-page copies into the WAL; crash recovery takes longer |
| `random_page_cost` | 4 | 1.1 on SSD | 4 prices a random read like a spinning disk, so the planner shuns index scans |
| `log_min_duration_statement` | -1, off | 250ms to 1s | logs every statement slower than that, with its duration |

sections.h: pg_hba.conf: the first matching line decides who gets in
sections.body:
`listen_addresses` decides where the server listens, and anyone who can reach that port can try to log in. Before it asks for a password, the new backend looks the connection up in `pg_hba.conf` (host-based authentication), in the data directory. Each line has five columns: how the client connected, which database, which role, from which address, and the method. These are the rules of the course's Docker image:

```text
local   all             all                                     trust
host    all             all             127.0.0.1/32            trust
host    all             all             ::1/128                 trust
local   replication     all                                     trust
host    replication     all             127.0.0.1/32            trust
host    replication     all             ::1/128                 trust
host    all             all             all                     scram-sha-256
```

The backend reads from the top, and **the first line that matches decides**. No later line is read: if that line asks for a password and the password is wrong, the client is refused, even if a later line would have trusted it. If no line matches, the client gets `no pg_hba.conf entry for host ...`. So specific lines go first and broad ones last, and a broad line in the wrong place locks people out: `host all all 0.0.0.0/0 reject` at the top refuses every IPv4 client, your own admin session included.

The columns:

- type: `local` is the Unix socket, for clients on the same machine; `host` is TCP with or without TLS; `hostssl` matches only TLS connections and `hostnossl` only plain ones.
- database and user: a name, a list (`payments,ledger`), `all`, or `+ops` for every member of role ops. `all` never matches a replication connection; a standby needs a line with the keyword `replication` (lesson 16).
- address: a CIDR block, an address plus how many of its leading bits must match. `10.20.0.0/16` is 10.20.0.0 to 10.20.255.255, and `/32` is one address. An IPv4 block never matches an IPv6 client, and `psql -h localhost` often connects from `::1`, past any `127.0.0.1/32` line.
- method: `scram-sha-256` proves the password without sending it (the default way passwords are stored since PostgreSQL 14; MD5 passwords are deprecated in 18); `peer` takes the OS user name on the socket as proof; `cert` checks a TLS client certificate; `trust` asks nothing; `reject` refuses.

`trust` from 127.0.0.1 is fine in a laptop container and nowhere else. On a server you want `peer` on the socket for the administrators, `hostssl ... scram-sha-256` or `cert` from each application network, and a last line that rejects the rest.

The server reads the file at start and on every reload. `SELECT * FROM pg_hba_file_rules` parses the file as it is now, with an `error` column for each line the server cannot read, so check it before you reload. A reload of a file with errors keeps the old rules (the log says `pg_hba.conf was not reloaded`), and a server started with one does not start at all. Keep one session open while you reload and test with a second connection before you close it. The open session stays in even if the new rules shut everyone else out.

sections.h: Roles: an owner, an application role, and nothing more
sections.body:
PostgreSQL has one kind of account, the **role**. A role with the `LOGIN` attribute can connect, and `CREATE USER name` is `CREATE ROLE name LOGIN`. A role without it works as a group: `GRANT ops TO asha` makes asha a member, and she gets what ops may do. Roles belong to the whole cluster (they live in `global/`). Every table belongs to a role too: whoever creates it owns it, and only the owner, or a superuser, can ALTER or DROP it.

The Docker image gives you one role to log in as, `sfz`, and it is a superuser: it skips every privilege check. A payments service that logs in as it can do whatever a bug or an injected statement asks, `DROP TABLE payments` or reading every customer's email. The fix is two roles with two jobs:

```sql
CREATE ROLE ledger_owner NOLOGIN;                 -- owns the schema and its tables; nobody logs in as it
CREATE SCHEMA ledger AUTHORIZATION ledger_owner;  -- migrations run as an admin after SET ROLE ledger_owner
CREATE ROLE payments_app LOGIN PASSWORD '...';    -- the service
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA ledger TO payments_app;     -- it may look up objects in the schema
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON ledger.payments, ledger.refunds TO payments_app;
GRANT INSERT ON ledger.audit_log TO payments_app; -- append-only: no SELECT, UPDATE or DELETE
```

A privilege is one verb on one object: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, and since PostgreSQL 17 MAINTAIN (VACUUM, ANALYZE, REINDEX). psql's `\dp payments` prints them as letters: `payments_app=arw/sfz` is INSERT (append), SELECT (read) and UPDATE (write), granted by sfz. No GRANT gives DROP; it comes with ownership. A refused statement fails with SQLSTATE 42501, `permission denied for table audit_log`.

Two traps. `GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA ledger` covers the tables that exist today, so the table next week's migration adds is closed to the app. `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE ledger_owner IN SCHEMA ledger GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON TABLES TO payments_app` sets the grants for tables ledger_owner creates later; `FOR ROLE` must name the role that will run the CREATE TABLE. The second trap is the `public` schema. Up to PostgreSQL 14, every role could create tables in it. Since 15 it belongs to `pg_database_owner` and everyone else only gets USAGE (`=U/pg_database_owner` in `\dn+`), but a database upgraded from 14 keeps the old rule until you run `REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA public FROM PUBLIC`. For a reporting role, grant the predefined role `pg_read_all_data` (PostgreSQL 14) instead of listing tables.

Row-level security narrows this to rows. `ALTER TABLE payments ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` and `CREATE POLICY merchant_rows ON payments USING (merchant_id = current_setting('app.merchant_id')::bigint)` make every query on the table see only the rows the policy allows, as if its condition were added to the WHERE clause. With RLS on and no policy, a role sees no rows at all. The table's owner, superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS skip policies unless the owner sets `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. It suits tenant isolation inside one table; it does not replace the GRANTs.

sections.h: Each connection is a process, so pool them
sections.body:
pgbench, which ships with PostgreSQL, measures what a connection costs. Eight clients run lookups by primary key for 10 seconds, first on connections that stay open, then with a new connection for every transaction (`-C`), in the course's container:

| clients connect over | connections stay open | a new one per transaction | average time to connect |
|---|---|---|---|
| the Unix socket, trust | 46,307 tps | 1,218 tps | 3.2 ms |
| TCP, scram-sha-256 | 33,428 tps | 270 tps | 14.7 ms |

A new connection costs a fork, the login and cold caches, and SCRAM is slow on purpose: it hashes the password 4,096 times (`scram_iterations`) so that a stolen hash is expensive to crack. Lesson 14 ("SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations") saw the same from Kotlin: 12 to 55 ms to open, under 1 ms per query after.

An open connection costs memory even when idle. In ps each backend showed about 18 MB of RSS, but most of that is shared memory and program code that every process maps; its private memory (`Private_Dirty` in `/proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup`) was 1.5 MB after one small query. Don't add up RSS. Private memory grows with use: catalog caches for each table touched, cached plans, and `work_mem` while a sort runs.

`max_connections` caps the processes. With 97 connections open on this server an ordinary role got `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute`, and at 100 even sfz got `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already`. Raising the cap to 2,000 makes that error go away and lets 2,000 processes fight over the same few cores, the slowdown lesson 14's pool sizing was about.

So keep server connections few and busy. For one service, its own pool, sized by lesson 14's formula. When many pods or services share one server, their pools add up, and a **connection pooler** goes in between. PgBouncer is the usual one: clients connect to it, on port 6432, and it holds a small set of server connections. In transaction pooling mode it lends a server connection to a client for one transaction only, so 1,000 client connections can share 40 server connections.

That breaks anything a session keeps between transactions, because the next transaction may run on another server connection: `SET` without `LOCAL`, `LISTEN`, session advisory locks, temporary tables kept across transactions, `WITH HOLD` cursors and SQL-level `PREPARE`. Protocol-level prepared statements, which pgJDBC switches to on the fifth run of a PreparedStatement, work since PgBouncer 1.21 if `max_prepared_statements` is above 0. The service itself barely changes:

```kotlin
HikariConfig().apply {
    jdbcUrl = "jdbc:postgresql://pgbouncer:6432/payments"   // PgBouncer, not db:5432
    username = "payments_app"
    maximumPoolSize = 10        // client connections to PgBouncer: cheap, it shares 40 server ones
    // only if PgBouncer is older than 1.21 or max_prepared_statements = 0:
    addDataSourceProperty("prepareThreshold", "0")   // no server-side prepared statements
}
```

A checklist for one production server:

- `listen_addresses` on the interfaces the apps use, and port 5432 reachable from nowhere else.
- pg_hba.conf with `peer` on the socket for admins, `hostssl ... scram-sha-256` or `cert` per application network and a final `reject`, checked in `pg_hba_file_rules` before every reload.
- shared_buffers at 25% of RAM, effective_cache_size at 50 to 75%, work_mem multiplied out, random_page_cost 1.1 on SSD, and one planned restart for the postmaster settings.
- max_wal_size and checkpoint_timeout large enough that the log shows `checkpoint starting: time`, not `wal` (log_checkpoints is on by default since 15).
- log_min_duration_statement set and pg_stat_statements loaded.
- an owner role per schema, a login role per service with default privileges, no service as superuser, and CREATE on public revoked in databases upgraded from 14 or older.
- pools that add up to well under max_connections, and PgBouncer when they don't.
- page checksums on (the default since 18), plus backups and a standby: lesson 16.

refs.title: PgBouncer: Features (pool modes, what transaction pooling supports)

analogy: Think of the server as an office building. The postmaster is the front desk: it does no work itself. It checks each visitor against a list taped to the counter, read from the top, where the first line that fits decides (pg_hba.conf), and then hires a personal assistant for that visitor alone (a backend process) for as long as they stay. All the assistants share one big filing room (shared_buffers), and each has a small desk of their own (work_mem). A badge says which drawers a visitor may open (roles and GRANTs), and only the owner of a cabinet may throw it out. The analogy breaks at the hiring: a new assistant here takes a few milliseconds, which sounds cheap until 2,000 visitors arrive at once, and the building has room for only `max_connections` assistants, however small their desks.
in_your_world: In a Quarkus service the pool is Agroal (`quarkus.datasource.jdbc.max-size`), and the server sees one backend process per pooled connection, per pod: twelve pods with 20 each are 240 processes, past the default `max_connections` of 100, which is when pods start failing with `remaining connection slots are reserved`. Give Flyway its own login, a member of the owner role that runs `SET ROLE ledger_owner` first (Flyway's `initSql`), and the service a login role with SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE, so a bad deploy cannot drop the ledger. A Kafka consumer group or a Temporal worker fleet that scales out multiplies connections the same way; that is the point to add PgBouncer, and to check that nothing uses session-level `SET` or advisory locks. Oracle at work runs a dedicated server process per session too, unless the DBA set up shared servers or DRCP, which pool inside the database. On a managed PostgreSQL such as RDS or Cloud SQL you change settings through a parameter group instead of postgresql.conf, and you get a role with most superuser powers but not all.
mistake: Letting the application log in as the superuser, or as the role that owns the tables. It happens because the Docker image, the tutorial and the first migration all use one role, and everything works. Then a migration with a wrong DROP, an ORM schema-update flag left on, or one injected statement can drop the payments table, and a bug in a reporting endpoint can read every customer's email. Make a NOLOGIN owner role for the schema, run migrations as it, give each service a LOGIN role with only the verbs it uses on only its tables, set default privileges FOR ROLE the owner so new tables follow, and test the refusals (42501) the way the lab does.

compare.note: Both run one process per session by default, so a connection is expensive on both. Oracle can change that inside the database, with threaded execution or pooled shared servers and DRCP; PostgreSQL cannot, so pooling has to happen in the application or in PgBouncer. The access check is split differently: Oracle's listener decides which networks may reach the database and the database checks the password, while PostgreSQL does both in pg_hba.conf, line by line, in the new backend before it runs anything. And an Oracle user is its schema, while a PostgreSQL schema is a namespace with an owner, which is what makes the owner role plus application role pattern easy.

ALTER SYSTEM SET max_connections = 200;                  -- with PgBouncer in front

lab.title: A pg_hba.conf evaluator, a settings reader, and a role that can only do its job
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. 23 of the 29 fail. `HbaTest` needs no database; `SettingsTest` and `LeastPrivilegeTest` run against PostgreSQL 18 in a container.

`Hba.kt` models pg_hba.conf. `parse` and `ipBytes` are given. Write `inCidr` first (the bit comparison), then `decide`: walk the lines, and let the first line whose type, database, user and address all match decide. The tests include the lockout, the IPv6 `localhost`, `all` against a standby, and the Docker image's own file with the Try it's reject line on top.

`Settings.kt` reads the real server: map each `pg_settings.context` to `HowToChange`, read a list of settings in the order asked, and list the names with `pending_restart`. Two tests run ALTER SYSTEM and `pg_reload_conf()` against the container and check what changed.

`least_privilege.sql` is what was shipped in a hurry: `GRANT ALL ON ALL TABLES`. Read its comment for what payments_app must and must not do, and rewrite it. The tests log in as payments_app with its password, over TCP and scram-sha-256, and expect SQLSTATE 42501 for each refusal.
Run the tests until all 29 pass.
hints: `inCidr`: `val a = ipBytes(address)` and `val n = ipBytes(cidr.substringBefore('/'))`; if the sizes differ, false. For bit `i` of the prefix, `val mask = 0x80 ushr (i % 8)` and compare `a[i / 8].toInt() and mask` with the same bits of `n`.

`decide`: write four small functions, one per column, and return at the first line where all four say yes. For a replication attempt, the database column matches only the keyword `replication`; `+ops` matches the user ops and any user with ops in `memberOf`.

`read`: `SELECT name, setting, unit, context, pending_restart FROM pg_settings WHERE name = ANY (?)` with `ps.setArray(1, conn.createArrayOf("text", names.toTypedArray()))`. Collect the rows into a map by name, then map `names` in order and throw for a missing one.

Roles: list the verbs per table (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE on payments and refunds; INSERT alone on audit_log), then add `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE ledger_owner IN SCHEMA ledger GRANT ... ON TABLES TO payments_app`. Without `FOR ROLE ledger_owner`, the default applies to tables the superuser creates, and the chargebacks test fails.

drill.title: A read-only role and its pg_hba.conf line, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the SQL that creates a login role `reports` that can read every table in schema `ledger`, including tables that `ledger_owner` creates later, and nothing else. Then write the pg_hba.conf line that lets it connect to database `payments` from 10.40.0.0/24 with a password, over TLS only, and say where in the file the line goes and what makes it take effect.

recap: A PostgreSQL server is a postmaster that forks one backend process per connection, a few helper processes (checkpointer, background writer, WAL writer, autovacuum, io workers), and shared memory with shared_buffers that every backend uses. work_mem and caches are private to each backend.

initdb creates the data directory: `base/` with one folder per database, `global/`, `pg_wal/` and the config files. ALTER SYSTEM writes postgresql.auto.conf, which overrides postgresql.conf; `-c` on the command line overrides both.
`pg_settings.context` says how a change applies: postmaster needs a restart, sighup a reload, superuser and user can also be SET per session. After a reload, `pending_restart` lists what still waits.

pg_hba.conf is read from the top, and the first line that matches type, database, user and address decides, with no fall-through. Specific lines first, a reject last, both address families covered, and `pg_hba_file_rules` checked before every reload.

Give each service a LOGIN role with only the verbs it uses, keep ownership (and so DROP) with a NOLOGIN owner role, and set ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE the owner for future tables. Refusals fail with 42501.

A new connection costs milliseconds and an idle one about a megabyte or two of private memory. Keep server connections few, pool in the application, and put PgBouncer in front when many pods add up, after checking for session state.

quiz.q: pg_hba.conf has `host all all 10.0.0.0/8 scram-sha-256` on line 1 and `host payments payments_app 10.20.0.0/16 trust` on line 2. The payments service connects from 10.20.3.4 with a wrong password. What happens?
options: It gets in: PostgreSQL uses the most specific matching line, line 2
It is refused: line 1 matched first, its password check failed, and PostgreSQL never reads line 2
It gets in after line 1 fails, because PostgreSQL falls through to the next matching line
It is refused with `no pg_hba.conf entry`, because two lines match
quiz.why: The first line whose type, database, user and address match is the only one used. 10.20.3.4 is inside 10.0.0.0/8, so line 1 decides: SCRAM, a wrong password, refused with 28P01. There is no fall-through and no most-specific rule. To trust that subnet you would have to move line 2 above line 1, which is also how a broad line in the wrong place locks everyone out.

quiz.q: You run `ALTER SYSTEM SET shared_buffers = '8GB'` and `SELECT pg_reload_conf()`. `SHOW shared_buffers` still says 128MB. What is going on?
options: shared_buffers has the context postmaster: the reload only set pending_restart, and the new value applies after a restart
ALTER SYSTEM failed silently; edit postgresql.conf by hand instead
The reload is asynchronous; wait a minute and SHOW will change
postgresql.auto.conf is only read by standbys
quiz.why: ALTER SYSTEM wrote the value into postgresql.auto.conf, and the reload made every process reread it. For a postmaster setting that only flags `pending_restart` and logs that the parameter cannot be changed without restarting: the buffer pool is shared memory the postmaster allocated at start. Editing postgresql.conf by hand would end the same way, and waiting changes nothing. Restart in a quiet moment, then SHOW says 8GB.

quiz.q: To stop a nightly report from spilling to disk, a team sets `work_mem = '512MB'` for the whole server: 64 GB of RAM, 200 connections. At the next traffic peak the kernel's OOM killer ends a backend, and every session is disconnected. Why?
options: work_mem is one limit for the whole server, so it cannot exceed 512 MB
work_mem comes out of shared_buffers, which shrank to make room
work_mem applies to each sort or hash in each backend, so many backends running plans with several of them can use many times 512 MB at once
The OOM killer targets any process that uses more than 512 MB
quiz.why: Every sort and every hash node in every running query may use up to work_mem (a hash twice that, with hash_mem_multiplier = 2). Two hundred backends with two hash joins each could ask for 400 GB. When the kernel kills one backend, the postmaster ends all the others too, because the dead process may have left shared memory half-written. Keep the server default small and raise it for the report alone: `ALTER ROLE reports SET work_mem = '512MB'`, or `SET work_mem` inside the report's session.

quiz.q: A month ago the reporting role got `GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA ledger TO reports`. Today a migration, run as ledger_owner, added `ledger.chargebacks`, and the report fails on it with SQLSTATE 42501. What lets every future table through without a GRANT per migration?
options: Run the same GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES once more; from then on it includes new tables
Make reports the owner of schema ledger
`ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA ledger GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO reports`, run as the superuser
`ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE ledger_owner IN SCHEMA ledger GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO reports`
quiz.why: ON ALL TABLES grants on the tables that exist when it runs, so running it again only fixes today. Default privileges apply to objects created later by one role, the one named in FOR ROLE; without it, they belong to the role running the statement, the superuser, who is not the one creating the tables. Ownership would hand the reporting role DROP and ALTER, the opposite of least privilege.

quiz.q: Lesson 14 sized one service's pool from the database's cores. Now 30 pods each run a Hikari pool of 10 against one 8-core PostgreSQL with `max_connections = 100`, and new pods fail with `remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute`. What do you change?
options: Raise max_connections to 400 so every pod fits
Put PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front, with a server pool of a few dozen connections, after checking the service keeps no session state (SET, LISTEN, advisory locks)
Make the service's role a superuser so it can use the reserved slots
Lower connectionTimeout so the pods give up sooner
quiz.why: 300 client connections means 300 backend processes for 8 cores: raising the cap trades an error for a slower server, the thrashing lesson 14's formula avoids. PgBouncer lets the 300 client connections share a small set of server connections, one transaction at a time, which breaks only session state between transactions. A superuser application is this lesson's mistake, and a shorter timeout fails faster without adding capacity.

flashcards.front: What does the postmaster do when a client connects?
flashcards.back: It forks a backend process that serves that one connection until the client disconnects. The postmaster itself never runs queries.

flashcards.front: postgresql.conf, postgresql.auto.conf, `-c` on the command line: which wins?
flashcards.back: `-c` beats both; postgresql.auto.conf (written by ALTER SYSTEM, read second) beats postgresql.conf.

flashcards.front: How do you tell whether a setting needs a restart?
flashcards.back: `SELECT context FROM pg_settings WHERE name = '...'`: postmaster needs a restart, sighup a reload; user and superuser can also be SET in a session. After a reload, `pending_restart` shows what still waits.

flashcards.front: Line 1 of pg_hba.conf matches, and the password is wrong. Does PostgreSQL try line 2?
flashcards.back: No. The first matching line decides; there is no fall-through. The client is refused.

flashcards.front: Why can `psql -h localhost` get past a `host ... 127.0.0.1/32 reject` line?
flashcards.back: localhost may connect from ::1, and an IPv4 entry never matches an IPv6 client.

flashcards.front: What does ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES change?
flashcards.back: The grants on objects created later by the role named in FOR ROLE (or the current role). Objects that exist keep theirs.

flashcards.front: What breaks behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode?
flashcards.back: Session state between transactions: SET without LOCAL, LISTEN, session advisory locks, WITH HOLD cursors, temp tables kept across transactions, SQL PREPARE.

terms.plain: The first PostgreSQL process: it listens for connections, owns shared memory and forks every other process.
The server process forked for one client connection; it runs that client's queries until it disconnects.
PostgreSQL's buffer pool: table and index pages cached in shared memory, used by every backend.
The one directory that holds a cluster's databases, WAL and config files; initdb creates it.
One data directory and the server running on it: a set of databases, roles and settings.
The file of rules, read from the top, that decides whether and how each connection must authenticate.
PostgreSQL's account: with LOGIN it can connect; without it, it groups privileges for its members.
A process such as PgBouncer that lets many client connections share a few server connections.

explain_back.prompt: At the evening peak the payments database starts refusing connections, and someone proposes setting max_connections to 2,000. Explain to them what a connection is on the server, what it costs, and what you would do instead.
explain_back.answer: On PostgreSQL every connection is a process. The postmaster forks a backend for each client, the backend checks pg_hba.conf and the password, and then it stays alive, holding its own memory, until the client disconnects. Opening one cost 3 to 15 ms in our measurement, and an idle one about 1.5 MB of private memory, more as it caches catalog entries and plans, and every sort in a query it runs can take work_mem on top. The refusals mean the pods' pools add up to more than max_connections. Raising the cap to 2,000 would replace the error with 2,000 processes competing for a handful of cores, and with a work_mem worst case nobody has multiplied out. I'd first add up the pools and shrink each one toward what the cores can serve, as lesson 14 did. If many pods still need many client connections, I'd put PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode in front, with a few dozen server connections, after checking that the service doesn't rely on session-level SET, LISTEN or advisory locks, and with max_prepared_statements set for pgJDBC's prepared statements.

deeper.body:
Why processes and not threads? A backend that crashes, from a bug in an extension or a segfault, cannot be trusted not to have scribbled on shared memory. So when any backend dies abnormally, the postmaster tells every other backend to exit, reinitializes shared memory and runs crash recovery from the WAL. Every session drops for a few seconds, but no damage spreads. Separate processes also let the kernel account for and kill one session at a time. The price is the fork and the per-process memory this lesson measured.

The Linux OOM killer prefers big processes, and in PostgreSQL's case killing one backend restarts all of them. The PostgreSQL documentation recommends `vm.overcommit_memory = 2` on dedicated database servers, so an allocation fails with an error in one query instead of the kernel killing a process later (see "Managing kernel resources", Linux memory overcommit). In containers, give the database a memory limit that covers shared_buffers plus the worst case of work_mem you allow.

Huge pages: shared_buffers is one big mapping, and with 4 KB pages the kernel's page tables for 8 GB of it, multiplied by every backend that touches it, cost real memory and TLB misses. `huge_pages = try` (the default) uses 2 MB pages if the kernel has them reserved; `SHOW shared_memory_size_in_huge_pages` tells you how many to reserve with `vm.nr_hugepages`.

Configuration management and ALTER SYSTEM can fight: Ansible writes postgresql.conf, and a DBA's ALTER SYSTEM silently overrides it from postgresql.auto.conf. PostgreSQL 17 added `allow_alter_system = off` for servers whose config is owned by a tool.

pg_hba.conf has more than this lesson used: `include_dir` for a directory of rule files, `@file` lists of roles, regular expressions with a leading slash (PostgreSQL 16), `pg_ident.conf` maps for `peer` and `cert`, and the `oauth` method in PostgreSQL 18, which validates bearer tokens through a validator library.

Log what reaches the front door: `log_connections` became a list in PostgreSQL 18, for example `log_connections = 'receipt,authentication,authorization,setup_durations'`, and the last option logs how long each stage of a new connection took, the same costs pgbench measured.
